title: Defense stocks: how to analyze defense contractors
description: Defense stocks: the state as customer and contracts spanning decades. How to calculate backlog coverage, margins and risks — with SIPRI's numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Defense stocks are shares in companies that develop, manufacture and maintain military materiel — aircraft, submarines, missile systems, radar, ammunition — and the services around them. The industry differs analytically from nearly all others: the customer is ultimately a single party, the state; contracts run for decades; and demand is governed by geopolitics and budget decisions rather than the business cycle. World military expenditure reached around 2,700 billion dollars in 2024, an increase of 9.4 percent — the largest annual increase since at least the end of the Cold War — according to SIPRI's military expenditure database, with the fastest increases in Europe. This guide walks through what that means for analysis: the backlog as the industry's most important number, the logic of margins, valuation — and the risks specific to defense stocks. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What defense stocks are — the state as customer

The business model in one sentence: recurring revenue from government customers through long, regulated contracts. The strong side is customer quality. The state is a creditworthy buyer, and a program won once is followed by decades of upgrades, spare parts and training — Gripen aircraft delivered in the 1990s are still maintained and developed by the manufacturer. That is aftermarket revenue with a longer horizon than most industries ever see. The demanding side is the customer's number and power. A country can choose among few approved suppliers, and the supplier can in practice sell only to states. Terms are set in procurements where price is squeezed, and every major export deal requires political approval.

Barriers to new competition form the industry's moat: security requirements, classified technology, approved-supplier status and decades of systems knowledge. The industry divides roughly into integrators that build entire systems — in Europe for example Saab in Sweden, BAE Systems in the United Kingdom and Rheinmetall in Germany — and subcontractors that supply components and services to several of them. The company names illustrate the industry's structure, not valuations of individual stocks.

## Demand — SIPRI's numbers and NATO's target

What drives an entire industry? World military expenditure has risen year after year since 2015, and NATO's summit in The Hague in June 2025 decided that the member states should reach five percent of GDP in defense and defense-related spending by 2035 — of which three and a half percent goes to core defense. That is a tightening of the two percent target from Wales in 2014. Sweden became a NATO member in March 2024 and has raised its allocations step by step toward two percent of GDP as a floor level in its defense bills. The point for analysis: demand for defense materiel is politically decided, multi-year and visible in public budgets — in the language of analysis, a high degree of [revenue stability](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys). The difference from a cyclical industry: the order flow does not depend on the consumer's mood but on threat perceptions and parliamentary majorities.

But note the word politically. What is decided politically can also be changed politically. A lasting security order would turn demand downward faster than the backlog has built up — the industry's most real long-term risk, and it shows up in no key ratio.

## The backlog — the most important number in defense analysis

The backlog (Swedish: orderstock) is the aggregate value of signed contracts not yet delivered and invoiced. Because revenue is recognized progressively as deliveries take place, the backlog says more about the future than last year's income statement. The key measure is coverage: the backlog divided by annual revenue.

A worked example at the level of the industry's Swedish heavyweight: a company with a backlog around 190 billion kronor and annual revenue of about 65 billion — levels in line with Saab's interim reporting 2026 — has coverage of 190 ÷ 65 ≈ 2.9. Nearly three years of production is already sold. That is how you calculate it; interpretation is made against the industry's normal range and the company's own history.

The backlog should be read in three dimensions. The level: how many years of revenue are booked. The growth: are orders received larger than recognized revenue — the measure is book-to-bill, where above 1.0 means the backlog is growing. And composition: in Sweden many defense agreements are signed as frame and option agreements, where a frame is only a ceiling and option rights must be exercised to become orders — the difference between signed frame and effective backlog is a classic note-reading moment. The tools for reading the order book are collected in the course [Order book and pricing](/kurser/km-069-orderbok-och-prissattning).

## The key ratios in the right order

For defense companies, key ratios are read in a different order than for software companies. First revenue stability and the backlog — they define the outlook. Then the margin: materiel integrators have historically landed in a span of 8–12 percent operating margin (Saab around 9–11 percent during the 2020s), while specialized subcontractors often sit higher. A worked example: operating income of 6.5 billion on revenue of 65 billion gives the margin 6.5 ÷ 65 = 10.0 percent — the span's midpoint.

Then capital binding. Development costs for a new system are enormous and bear fruit only years later, which makes the return on capital employed a measure of how well the company chooses its programs — the technique runs through [how to calculate ROE](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe). The balance sheet has an industry-specific subtlety: customer prepayments mean cash flow often runs ahead of the income statement, producing seemingly high cash — the difference between prepayments and earned revenue lives in the notes, and the threshold for dangerous indebtedness is walked through in [debt-to-equity levels](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig). Valuation comes last: P/E and EV/EBIT are set against the company's own history and against the backlog's coverage — the tools are in the [EV/EBIT course](/kurser/km-010-evebit) and [relative valuation](/kurser/km-011-relativ-vardering).

## Three risks that are specific to defense stocks

- **The political cycle.** Threat perceptions and majorities steer the budgets. Rearmament is decided for years, not decades, and a changed security policy strikes directly at the order flow.
- **The export controls.** Every major cross-border deal requires permits — in the United States through ITAR, in Sweden through national export review. A stopped or delayed export can freeze revenue already counted into the backlog. The regulatory mechanics go deeper in [regulatory analysis](/blogg/v18-regulatoriska-analys).
- **The concentration.** Few customers, few programs. A company whose identity rests on one dominant system — like Saab on Gripen — has a clear single-point risk: a cancelled program shows up in the backlog immediately. Some funds also exclude the industry on ethical grounds, which shapes the shareholder base and can affect the valuation without affecting the business itself.

## Valuation — what is already priced in

Europe's defense stocks were repriced sharply between 2022 and 2026; several companies went from low multiples to a premium over the market at large. For analysis, the central question is therefore not whether the rearmament is real — it is — but how much of it already sits in the prices. Three tools: the multiple against the company's own history (five years say more than twelve months), EV/EBIT against the backlog's coverage, and caution with PEG ratios — growth driven by a one-time rearmament can look structural until the cycle turns, taken apart in [the weaknesses of the PEG multiple](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026).

## The summary

- The defense industry's customer is the state: creditworthy, few and political — long contracts, a wide moat, an uneven negotiating position.
- The backlog is the key ratio: coverage 190 ÷ 65 ≈ 2.9 years in the example; read level, growth (book-to-bill) and composition (frames versus option rights).
- The margins have historically been around 8–12 percent for integrators; capital binding and customer prepayments shape the balance sheet.
- Industry-specific risks: the political cycle, the export controls and the concentration on few programs and customers.
- Valuation against history and backlog — with the question of what is already priced in always open.

The next step in the education track: the course [the defense sector](/kurser/se-03-forsvarssektorn) goes through the industry's analysis in six chapters, [how to read a Swedish annual report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-svensk-arsredovisning) trains the note-reading where backlog details live, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) places the method in the whole.

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
